19.1 Your Environment and Functions
Consider this notebook more an “FYI”, the content won’t be tested directly, but understanding how scoping works may help you troubleshoot your code!
Functions in R return an object. In general, R functions are and should be designed such that the only effect of the function is through the return value.
Side effects are when a function affects the state of the world in addition to its return value. Can you think of any side effects that you saw an R function produce from earlier in the workshop? What about:
Functions in R are (roughly) pass-by-value and not pass-by-reference. This means that if you modify an argument inside the function it will not change the original value outside the function. This protects you from a major potential source of side effects. (There are exceptions to this rule.)
In actuality, functions in R are call-by-value. What this means for our purposes is that you can pass an input argument in without a copy being made of it. This saves time and memory. At the time that you modify the input within the function (if ever), then a copy is made and the modified input is different than the original value outside the function.

title: 19  Variable Scoping
text:
19.2 Variable scope and global variables
In Lecture 1e, we saw that, when we call a function or other object, R looks for what this object refers to in this order:

The global environment
Sequentially up the search path

Functions also create their own environment, which lasts until the function finishes executing. When you refer to an object from within a function, the order becomes:

The function environment
The global environment
Sequentially up the search path

Here are a couple examples to illustrate:

# y is defined in the function:
add_to_y <- function(x) {
  y <- 8
  x + y
}

y <- 9
add_to_y(7)
#> [1] 15

In the example above, y is defined in the function (as 8) and so the value of 8 is used, even though the global value of y is 9.

# y is defined outside the function (this is considered bad practice)
add_to_y <- function(x) {
  x + y
}

y <- 9
add_to_y(7) 
#> [1] 16

In this example, the function environment does NOT contain a definition of y and so R looks for this object in the global environment, where it finds y <- 9.
There’s one more (advanced) case that is useful to know about.
Functions are defined with a reference to the environment in which they are created.

# Part 1: defining a function within a function scope
add_numbers <- function(x) {
  y <- 10
  add_to_y <- function(z) {
    z + y
  }
  # call the function we just defined:
  return(add_to_y(z = x))
}

y <- 9
add_numbers(7)
#> [1] 17

What’s going on?
When we call add_to_y, R looks in the environment in which that function was defined, which is within the environment created by add_numbers, where y <- 10 – even though the global environment sets y <- 9.
Here’s one more advanced example:

# Part 2: defining a function within a global scope
y <- 10
add_to_y <- function(z) {
  z + y
}

# Define `y` within `add_numbers`
add_numbers <- function(x) {
  y <- 1000
  return(add_to_y(z = x))
}
add_numbers(7)
#> [1] 17

Here, add_to_y is defined in the global environment. When we call add_to_y, R looks for y in the following order:

The function environment of add_to_y –> no y is defined, so continue
The environment in which add_to_y is defined, the global environment.

If y did not exist in the global environment, R will next check our search path (which contains all the packages we have laoded.)
We can remove y from the global environment, and R will still not use the value y <- 1000.

20.2 Combining multiple data frames

20.2.1 left_join
Sometimes we need to use data available from multiple sources. To take advantage of the dplyr functions we used previously, we need data points of interest to be in the same data frame. The join family of functions helps here.

pt_char <- data.frame(
  pt = c("M.H.", "P.J.", "K.G.", "A.C."),
  age = c(77, 35, 56, 48),
  weight = c(65, 82, 70, 100),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
pt_char
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   pt      age weight
#>   <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 M.H.     77     65
#> 2 P.J.     35     82
#> 3 K.G.     56     70
#> 4 A.C.     48    100

pt_doses <- data.frame(
  pt = c("M.H.", "P.J.", "K.G.", "M.H.", "S.C."),
  mg_per_kg = c(15, 15, 10, 20, 15),
  interval = c("Q8", "Q12", "Q6", "Q8", "Q8"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
pt_doses
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   pt    mg_per_kg interval
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <chr>   
#> 1 M.H.         15 Q8      
#> 2 P.J.         15 Q12     
#> 3 K.G.         10 Q6      
#> 4 M.H.         20 Q8      
#> 5 S.C.         15 Q8

What happens if we want to calculate mg of drug per kg body weight?

# left_join adds all the data from the right df 
# to the matching rows of the left dataframe
?left_join
left_join(pt_char, pt_doses)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   pt      age weight mg_per_kg interval
#>   <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>   
#> 1 M.H.     77     65        15 Q8      
#> 2 M.H.     77     65        20 Q8      
#> 3 P.J.     35     82        15 Q12     
#> 4 K.G.     56     70        10 Q6      
#> 5 A.C.     48    100        NA <NA>

Note what happens to patient A.C., who does not have dosing information, and patient S.C., for whom we do not have patient characteristics. Also, see how R handled patient M.H., who was in the dosing table twice. Let’s try the reverse:

left_join(pt_doses, pt_char, by = "pt")
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   pt    mg_per_kg interval   age weight
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <chr>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 M.H.         15 Q8          77     65
#> 2 P.J.         15 Q12         35     82
#> 3 K.G.         10 Q6          56     70
#> 4 M.H.         20 Q8          77     65
#> 5 S.C.         15 Q8          NA     NA

What happened here to A.C., M.H. and S.C.?
What if we want to keep all entries?


20.2.2 full_join
Let’s compare full_join with left_join

full_join(pt_char, pt_doses)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   pt      age weight mg_per_kg interval
#>   <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>   
#> 1 M.H.     77     65        15 Q8      
#> 2 M.H.     77     65        20 Q8      
#> 3 P.J.     35     82        15 Q12     
#> 4 K.G.     56     70        10 Q6      
#> 5 A.C.     48    100        NA <NA>    
#> 6 S.C.     NA     NA        15 Q8


# R will do its best guess to try judge which columns you want to join on if you
# do not otherwise specify. Here, the names match, but not all data is so
# convenient. Here's a contrived example:
pt_doses |>
  rename(patient = pt) |>
  left_join(pt_char, by = c("patient" = "pt")) 
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   patient mg_per_kg interval   age weight
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <chr>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 M.H.           15 Q8          77     65
#> 2 P.J.           15 Q12         35     82
#> 3 K.G.           10 Q6          56     70
#> 4 M.H.           20 Q8          77     65
#> 5 S.C.           15 Q8          NA     NA



20.2.3 right_join
Right join is the reverse of left_join.

right_join(pt_char, pt_doses)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   pt      age weight mg_per_kg interval
#>   <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>   
#> 1 M.H.     77     65        15 Q8      
#> 2 M.H.     77     65        20 Q8      
#> 3 P.J.     35     82        15 Q12     
#> 4 K.G.     56     70        10 Q6      
#> 5 S.C.     NA     NA        15 Q8
left_join(pt_doses, pt_char)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 5
#>   pt    mg_per_kg interval   age weight
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <chr>    <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 M.H.         15 Q8          77     65
#> 2 P.J.         15 Q12         35     82
#> 3 K.G.         10 Q6          56     70
#> 4 M.H.         20 Q8          77     65
#> 5 S.C.         15 Q8          NA     NA



20.2.4 inner_join
What if we want to keep only patients for whom we have complete information?

inner_join(pt_char, pt_doses) |>
  mutate(mg = mg_per_kg * weight)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   pt      age weight mg_per_kg interval    mg
#>   <chr> <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>    <dbl>
#> 1 M.H.     77     65        15 Q8         975
#> 2 M.H.     77     65        20 Q8        1300
#> 3 P.J.     35     82        15 Q12       1230
#> 4 K.G.     56     70        10 Q6         700

title: 20  Combining and Reshaping Data
text:
20.3 Tidyr: Long versus Wide Data
Even before we conduct analysis or calculations, we need to put our data into the correct format. The goal here is to rearrange a messy dataset into one that is tidy.
The two most important properties of tidy data are:

Each column is a variable.
Each row is an observation.

Tidy data is easier to work with, because you have a consistent way of referring to variables (as column names) and observations (as row indices). It then becomes easy to manipulate, visualize, and model.
Many tools in R will assume that your data is already tidy.
For more on the concept of tidy data, read Hadley Wickham’s paper here

20.3.1 Wide vs. Long Formats

“Tidy datasets are all alike but every messy dataset is messy in its own way.” – Hadley Wickham

Tabular datasets can be arranged in many ways. For instance, consider the data below. Each data set displays information on heart rate observed in individuals across 3 different time periods. But the data are organized differently in each table.

wide <- data.frame(
  name = c("Wilbur", "Petunia", "Gregory"),
  time1 = c(67, 80, 64),
  time2 = c(56, 90, 50),
  time3 = c(70, 67, 101)
)
wide
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   name    time1 time2 time3
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Wilbur     67    56    70
#> 2 Petunia    80    90    67
#> 3 Gregory    64    50   101

long <- data.frame(
  name = c(
    "Wilbur", "Petunia", "Gregory", "Wilbur", "Petunia", 
    "Gregory", "Wilbur", "Petunia", "Gregory"
  ),
  time = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3),
  heartrate = c(67, 80, 64, 56, 90, 50, 70, 67, 10)
)
long
#> # A tibble: 9 × 3
#>   name     time heartrate
#>   <chr>   <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Wilbur      1        67
#> 2 Petunia     1        80
#> 3 Gregory     1        64
#> 4 Wilbur      2        56
#> 5 Petunia     2        90
#> 6 Gregory     2        50
#> 7 Wilbur      3        70
#> 8 Petunia     3        67
#> 9 Gregory     3        10

Question: Which one of these do you think is the tidy format?
We often refer to these different structurs as “long” vs. “wide” formats. In the “long” format, you usually have 1 column for the observed variable and the other columns are ID variables.
For the “wide” format each row is often a site/subject/patient and you have multiple observation variables containing the same type of data. These can be either repeated observations over time, or observation of multiple variables (or a mix of both). In the above case, we had the same kind of data (heart rate) entered across 3 different columns, corresponding to three different time periods.

You may find data input may be simpler and some programs/functions may prefer the “wide” format. However, many of R’s functions have been designed assuming you have “long” format data.


20.3.2 From Wide to Long and Back
Here’s an example data set, which has the Billboard top 100 ranking for each song for each week in the year 2000.
How many weeks did each song spend on the Billboard top 100?

#>  3 3 Doors Down   Kryptonite       2000-04-08      81    70    68    67    66
#>  4 3 Doors Down   Loser            2000-10-21      76    76    72    69    67

Having each week as a column is convenient if you want to sort the song by their position in a given week.
On the other hand, there are some instances in which a purely long or wide format is ideal (e.g. plotting). Likewise, sometimes you’ll get data on your desk that is poorly organized, and you’ll need to reshape it.


20.3.3 tidyr
Thankfully, the tidyr package will help you efficiently transform your data regardless of original format.

# Load the "tidyr" package (necessary every new R session)
library(tidyr)



20.3.4 tidyr::pivot_longer
The function pivot_longer() will turn a wide dataframe into a longer one by transforming the observation variables into a single variable. This is sometimes called “melting” your data, because it melts the table from wide to long. You might also see it called “gathering”.
Those data will be melted into two variables: one for the variable names, and the other for the variable values. Often, the terms “key” and “value” are used to refer to the variable names and variable values. You might also see the terms “name” and “value”.

?pivot_longer

billboard |>
  select(artist, track, starts_with("wk")) 
#> # A tibble: 317 × 78
#>    artist         track               wk1   wk2   wk3   wk4   wk5   wk6   wk7
#>    <chr>          <chr>             <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 2 Pac          Baby Don't Cry (…    87    82    72    77    87    94    99
#>  2 2Ge+her        The Hardest Part…    91    87    92    NA    NA    NA    NA
#>  3 3 Doors Down   Kryptonite           81    70    68    67    66    57    54
#>  4 3 Doors Down   Loser                76    76    72    69    67    65    55
#>  5 504 Boyz       Wobble Wobble        57    34    25    17    17    31    36
#>  6 98^0           Give Me Just One…    51    39    34    26    26    19     2
#>  7 A*Teens        Dancing Queen        97    97    96    95   100    NA    NA
#>  8 Aaliyah        I Don't Wanna        84    62    51    41    38    35    35
#>  9 Aaliyah        Try Again            59    53    38    28    21    18    16
#> 10 Adams, Yolanda Open My Heart        76    76    74    69    68    67    61
#> # ℹ 307 more rows
#> # ℹ 69 more variables: wk8 <dbl>, wk9 <dbl>, wk10 <dbl>, wk11 <dbl>, …

Notice that we put 3 arguments into the pivot_longer() function:

the name for the new column for the new ID variable (week),
the name for the new observation variable (position),
the names of the columns that we want to gather into one variable. (We could also have supplied the names of the columns we don’t want to re-shape, or the indices of these columns)

Notice that we don’t want to melt down columns 1 and 2, as these are considered “ID” variables.
We are nearly where we want to be. How many weeks did each song spend on the charts?


20.3.5 tidyr::pivot_wider
pivot_wider is the opposite of pivot_longer. It makes new columns using values in one column as the new column names, and the values in a second column as the new column values.
Usually, this means taking “tidy” data and making it “untidy”, but sometimes it is helpful to have data in this format for displaying in tables or plots.

20.4 tidyselect

  ETA1 = c(0.03, 0.03, -0.05, -0.05),

  ETA3 = c(-0.1, -0.1, 0.2, 0.2)

# how do I get just the columns that start with "ETA"?

B.1 Books
The focus of these lectures was to provide an introduction to R programming, not statistics. The remainder of the course will introduce you to a variety of statistical approaches. If you want to go beyond those lectures, the following resources are a great place to start!
Let’s start with some book recommendations:
All of these books are well-written, engaging, and have examples in R.2 Together they cover applications of fundamental and state-of-the-art tools in statistical modelling. But most importantly—they encourage statistical thinking. They’re ideal books for self-study and I can’t recommend them enough.

TipAll you need is the linear model



Most people have the unfortunate experience of learning statistics through arcane rituals with numerous statistical tests that appear to have no fundamental framework to tie them together. This is a failure of pedagogy rather than a feature of statistics. Fortunately, there is a fundamental framework to tie all these statistical tests together: It’s called the linear model.
Most common statistical tests are either special cases or extensions of the linear model; understanding this will improve your statistical thinking and make it easier to abandon the arcanum and statistical rituals in favour of a unified statistical framework.
For a short introduction to this concept I recommend reading Common statistical tests are linear models (or: how to teach stats) by Jonas Kristoffer Lindeløv (note: there are a few small errors that haven’t been fixed, so also see the GitHub Issues).

B.2 Course materials
A lot of people in the R community who have taught courses or workshops make their materials openly available (including your instructors!). One source I want to highlight in particular is psyTeachR from the University of Glasgow School of Psychology and Neuroscience, which covers an entire curriculum of courses for doing reproducible data science.
Michael McCarthy has also previously taught two graduate-level statistics courses in R at the University of Calgary Department of Psychology, which covered some of the topics in PHC 506:

PSYC 615: Analysis of Variance, which covered applications of the general linear model (t-tests, ANOVA) to research design and analysis.
PSYC 617: Multivariate Analysis, which covered applications of univariate and multivariate statistics to research design and analysis, including correlations, multiple regression, logistic regression, discriminant analysis, MANOVA, linear mixed models with nested and longitudinal designs, exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, path analysis, and structural equation modelling.
alda: He has also created an R data package for the book “Applied longitudinal data analysis: Modeling change and event occurrence” by Singer and Willett (2003), which includes chapter examples for longitudinal mixed effects modelling and survival analysis.

title: Appendix B — Statistics in R
text:
Regression and Other Stories is an updated and expanded second edition of the regressions parts of Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. The authors are also working on an updated and expanded second edition of the multilevel modelling parts of Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models, but it isn’t out yet.↩︎
Most of these books have also had their examples translated to use different R packages than the authors used. For example, Andrew Heiss has translated Bayes Rules! and Statistical Rethinking into the tidyverse, brms, and marginaleffects packages; Emil Hvitfeldt has translated An introduction to statistical learning into the tidymodels set of packages; and A. Solomon Kurz has translated Regression and Other Stories into the tidyverse and brms packages.↩︎

title: Appendix C — Additional Resources

C.1 Books
The lectures in this book are a starting point. The following books and references will help you keep learning and mastering R well beyond what we cover in class—they come highly recommended.

title: Appendix C — Additional Resources
text:
C.1.1 Hands-On Programming with R
This book teaches you how to program in R with hands-on examples. It was written for non-programmers as a friendly introduction to the language. You’ll learn how to load data, assemble and disassemble data objects, navigate R’s environment system, write your own functions, and use all of R’s programming tools — solving practical data science problems along the way.
A great place to start is the Preface and Chapter 1, which pair well with Lecture 1.


C.1.2 R for Data Science
This book teaches you how to do data science with R: how to get your data into R, put it into the most useful structure, transform it, visualize it, and model it. It covers the grammar of graphics, literate programming, and reproducible research, along with best practices for wrangling, visualizing, and exploring data.

title: Appendix C — Additional Resources
text:
C.2 Cheat sheets
For quick, printable references on individual packages such as dplyr and ggplot2, see Posit’s cheat sheet collection at https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/contributed-cheatsheets.html. A condensed summary of the functions used in this course is also in the R Cheat Sheet appendix.

title: Appendix C — Additional Resources
text:
C.3 Getting help
R has a large, welcoming community. When you get stuck, searching Stack Overflow or the relevant package’s GitHub issues will often turn up an answer—and R’s built-in help (?function_name) is always a good first stop.
